seen.where: Weber, Masked Dispatches (NSA 2013), govinfo PDF, ch. 17 text and notes 60-63, read in full for this item; E. C. Fishel, 'A Cable from Napoleon' (CIA Studies in Intelligence reprint of his NSA Technical Journal article of July 1958), https://cia.gov/resources/csi/static/A-Cable-from-Napoleon.pdf, text read in full. The CIA PDF carries the captions of the facsimiles but not the images, so no leaf of the cipher was seen.
seen.extent: one cable: Weber says '373-cable-word message'; Fishel says 'this one message of eighty-eight groups' on five pages of Western Union blanks
seen.cipher: Fishel: 'a copy of a coded telegram to Napoleon from Bazaine and Castelnau ... the message was in code and not cipher'; caption 'First and last pages of the five-page message to Napoleon III from his commanders in Mexico'. Weber n. 46 quotes the opening groups '2209 613 562 273 15 2214'.

prior_art.lasry: No Lasry paper or GL.htm item on the French Mexican-expedition code turned up in the three searches; not a Lasry target as far as found.
prior_art.edition: The clear text of this same message is in print: Girard, La vie et les souvenirs du general Castelnau (Paris 1930), pp. 117-118 (Castelnau repeated it in his letter to Napoleon of 8 Dec 1866), reprinted in French and in English translation by Fishel 1958 ('L'empereur Maximilien parait vouloir rester au Mexique, mais on ne peut y compter ...'). Girard itself was not opened; the French text was read in Fishel's reprint.
prior_art.literature: Fishel 1958 and Weber 2013 (n. 61: 'The actual message is reprinted by E. C. Fishel') both conclude that Keefer never solved the code; neither reconstructs any code group. No later reconstruction of the French code found.

633.key_check: No key to the French 1866 code is held in the repo, on DECODE or in print as far as found; Fishel thinks this was the only encrypted French cable of the intervention. Nothing tested: the code groups are not online beyond the six in Weber n. 46.

633.closed: The content is on record: the sender's own clear text of this cable is printed by Girard 1930 pp. 117-118 and reprinted with a translation by Fishel 1958 (CIA 'A Cable from Napoleon'). What is unsolved is the code, not the message: no group has been matched to the clear text. If kept, it is a known-plaintext code rebuild, not an unread document. Ciphertext location per Fishel n. 35: National Archives, filed with telegrams sent from the military headquarters at New Orleans 1864-69 (besides Keefer to Grant, 17 Dec 1866, Seward Papers reel 98); not online.

640.unvetted: Ciphertext not seen and the prior-art question cannot be closed without it. Seen (NARA M37 roll 2 image 0022, full JPEG, 9 Nov 2026): only the typed list of reports, with 'Part in cipher.' (10 May 1811) and 'Parts in cipher.' (25 and 30 Jul 1811); a pencilled word beside the 16 June entry may read 'Decoded'. These are the Department's received copies returned to Poinsett in 1818 (Manning vol. 1 preface, checked in the Internet Archive text), and the 1814 sibling of the same kind carries a clerk's decode over the groups (targets/poinsett1813), so the cipher parts may already be deciphered on the leaf. Manning vols. 1-2 (IA full text) print no Poinsett letter of 1811. The Heilman-Levin Calendar of the Poinsett papers in the Gilpin collection (1941, IA full text) covers a different HSP collection and has no 1811 report and no mention of cipher: the entry's 'Gilpin collection, vol. 4' is doubtful (the list says vol. 1 of the Poinsett Papers). Three web searches found no edition or decipherment. Entry access should be 'archive', not 'online'. Needs HSP images of the three reports.
